opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that locomotion is a problem where the physics is, in a sense, "simple enough" and "forgiving enough" for classical methods to work really well.

If you look at a quadruped walking, the main interaction with the world is the feet touching the ground. The contacts are relatively sparse: you have four feet, each either in contact or not, and the ground is mostly rigid and flat or at least predictable. So you can write down a fairly clean model of the robot's rigid-body dynamics, treat the contacts in a simplified way, and then do model predictive control or whole-body control on top of that. People like the MIT Cheetah team and others showed that with a good model and a fast optimizer, you get very robust, dynamic behaviors. And then when the field moved to sim-to-real reinforcement learning, locomotion was again a great fit, because the simulator could capture the dominant physics accurately enough: rigid bodies, point contacts, some friction. The sim-to-real gap was manageable with domain randomization.

Another factor is the objective. For locomotion, the goal is basically "keep your body stable and move in this direction." It's the same task over and over, and the robot is mostly dealing with its own body. You don't need to understand the world semantically. Balance is something the robot can sense through proprioception, joint encoders and an IMU, so you don't even necessarily need vision to do a lot of it.

Manipulation is very different. First, the contacts are rich and complicated. When you grasp something with a hand, you have many contact points, sliding, rolling, sticking, and they change constantly. Friction is hard to model; small errors in contact geometry make a huge difference. And the objects themselves are diverse: deformable things like cloth, cables, food, liquids, articulated objects like drawers and doors. Classical physics simulators are just not accurate for many of these, and even when they are, you need to know the object's mass, friction, shape, and so on, which you usually don't have in the real world.

Second, manipulation requires perception and understanding of the environment in a way locomotion doesn't. You need to know where the object is, what it is, how it should be handled, what the task even means. Every task is different: folding a shirt, loading a dishwasher, opening a bag. So you can't just engineer one controller and reuse it everywhere the way you can with a walking gait.

Third, the precision tolerance is different. If a leg lands a centimeter off, the robot just adapts on the next step; locomotion is periodic and self-correcting. In manipulation, if you're a few millimeters off, you miss the grasp or knock the object over, and the task fails.

So in short, locomotion is dominated by the robot's own dynamics with simple, repetitive contact, which physics-based modeling and simulation handle well. Manipulation is dominated by interaction with a diverse, hard-to-model world, and that's exactly where traditional physics-based approaches struggle. That's also why I think data-driven approaches, learning from real-world demonstrations, have become so important for manipulation specifically.

r001.rationale: It says friction is hard to model and that manipulation often requires knowing each object’s friction, tying friction variability and uncertainty to modeling difficulty.

r002.rationale: It describes quadruped contacts as sparse and simplified, but does not say ground contacts are brief or that this reduces the need to know contact friction in detail.

r003.rationale: It explains that manipulation requires knowledge of contact behavior and object properties such as mass, friction, and shape, which are often unavailable, while locomotion works with simpler, more predictable physics.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to how much of the problem you can actually write down.

With a quadruped, the thing you care about is mostly the robot's own body. You know its mass, its joint limits, how the legs move. The contact is with the ground, and the ground is comparatively forgiving: it's a surface, it pushes back, you can model friction well enough. So locomotion is really a problem about controlling the robot itself, and you can describe that with equations, build a dynamics model, and do things like model predictive control or trajectory optimization. The world is almost a parameter in that problem rather than the problem itself. That's why Boston Dynamics and the whole generation of legged robots got to such impressive results with largely physics-based methods, and why reinforcement learning on legged robots also took off so fast once sim-to-real matured — the simulator could be trusted because the physics was tractable.

Manipulation flips that. The hard part is no longer the robot, it's the object. You need to know what you're grasping, its shape, how heavy it is, whether it's rigid or deformable, how slippery it is, where it is relative to the hand. Contact is now rich and intermittent: fingers making and breaking contact, objects rotating in the hand, things sliding. Those contact dynamics are notoriously difficult to model, and even small errors compound quickly. And the number of distinct situations is essentially unbounded — every kitchen, every cup, every piece of cloth is different. A hand-written model can't enumerate that.

So in locomotion the physics-based approach was attacking a problem that was mostly in its domain of competence. In manipulation it was being asked to model perception, object understanding, and contact uncertainty all at once, and those are exactly the places where explicit models break down. That's also why manipulation is where learning from data has become so central — not because the physics is wrong, but because the relevant information lives in the world rather than in the robot, and you can only get at it by observing a lot of it.

r001.rationale: The response says an object’s slipperiness matters, but does not clearly identify variation in friction across objects as a specific modeling obstacle.

r002.rationale: It describes ground contact as comparatively forgiving and friction as modelable, but does not explain that brief ground contacts reduce the need for detailed friction knowledge.

r003.rationale: It attributes manipulation’s weaker results to the need to model many object properties, complex contact dynamics, perception, and uncertainty, unlike locomotion’s more tractable robot-centered physics.

astra-6.text:
I think a big reason is that locomotion has a relatively consistent structure. For a quadruped, you know the robot’s geometry, its joints, and roughly what contact with the ground looks like. You can build a physics model and use optimization and feedback control to keep it balanced. The terrain can change, but the basic task stays the same: make and break contact with the ground while moving the body.

Manipulation is much more open-ended. Every object can have a different shape, mass distribution, friction, or stiffness, and you often don’t know those properties in advance. As soon as you touch something, the contact can change: it might slide, rotate, deform, or slip out of your grasp. Small modeling errors can lead to very different outcomes.

So traditional physics-based approaches had a more tractable problem in quadruped locomotion. Those methods also work well for manipulation in structured settings, where objects and motions are predictable. The difficulty is getting that same reliability when the objects and interactions are unfamiliar.

r001.rationale: It says objects can differ in friction and that these properties are often unknown in advance, making manipulation harder to model.

r002.rationale: It describes making and breaking ground contact, but does not say those contacts are brief or that they reduce the need to know contact friction in detail.

r003.rationale: It contrasts locomotion’s tractable physics model with manipulation’s varied, often unknown physical properties and changing contacts, attributing manipulation’s difficulty to greater physical-modeling demands.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that locomotion gives you a relatively clean problem to model. You know the robot’s geometry, you can estimate its state, and you have a fairly clear objective: maintain balance and move at a desired velocity. Even though foot contact is complicated, you can often simplify it enough for a physics-based controller to work well. And you can keep adjusting the motion as new measurements come in.

Manipulation forces you to deal with much more of the unknown world. You pick up an object, and you may not know its mass, friction, stiffness, or even its exact shape. The contact can change from sticking to sliding, and a small error in where you touch can completely change the outcome. If you’re manipulating something deformable, the modeling problem becomes even harder.

So I wouldn’t say quadruped locomotion is easy. But the structure of the problem makes modeling and optimization particularly useful. With manipulation, a lot of the difficulty is in the object and the contact, and those are precisely the things your model often describes least accurately.

r001.rationale: The response says an object's friction may be unknown, but it does not identify friction variation across objects as the modeling obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says foot contact can be simplified, but does not explain that brief ground contacts reduce the need to know contact friction in detail.

r003.rationale: It attributes manipulation's weaker results to greater uncertainty about object properties and contact, which makes its physical models less accurate than those used for locomotion.
